subject: Cognitive Science
title: Language Attrition
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Language Attrition.

hook.text: An immigrant returns home after 20 years and finds her first language feels clumsy. She pauses, searches for words she once knew.

buildup.text: Language attrition is the gradual loss of a language you stop using. It begins with vocabulary and expression.

discovery.text: The first language doesn't vanish, though. Brain studies show it's still represented—just harder to access.

twist.text: Relearning a 'lost' language is dramatically faster than learning a new one. The pathways are dormant, not destroyed.

climax.text: If you learned the language before age 12, the core grammar typically survives attrition even decades later.

punchline.text: A neglected language fades but rarely dies.

quiz.question: What happens to a first language that stops being used?
options: It becomes harder to access but persists

details.summary: Language attrition is the gradual loss of a first language when a speaker is immersed in a second language environment. Vocabulary retrieval slows, grammar simplifies, and accent may shift.
details.whyItMatters: Attrition reveals that language knowledge is dynamic, not fixed. It has implications for immigrant communities, heritage language maintenance, and understanding memory systems.
takeaways: First language skills can erode with prolonged disuse
Vocabulary access is affected before grammar deteriorates
Emotional and early-acquired language is most resistant

faq.question: How quickly can a first language be lost?
faq.answer: Measurable changes in vocabulary retrieval can appear within three to five years of immersion in a new language. Children who emigrate before puberty are most vulnerable to severe attrition.

faq.question: Is an attrited language truly forgotten?
faq.answer: Probably not entirely. Savings studies show that relearning an attrited language is faster than learning from scratch, meaning traces remain. Re-immersion can reactivate dormant competence. The first language may be inhibited rather than erased, suppressed by the dominant second language.
